title: Closed subgroups of additive group powers over a perfect field have additive, infinitesimal and etale factors
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] of characteristic $p>0$ such that every element of $k$ is a $p$-th power. Let $n\geq0$ and let $H\subseteq\mathbf G_a^n$ be a closed subgroup scheme [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup] of the affine $k$-group scheme with coordinatewise addition [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sc-gm-ga]. Assume $H$ is of finite type over $k$ [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. There exist integers $d,s,a\geq0$, integers $r_1,\ldots,r_s\geq1$, a commutative finite etale $k$-group scheme $E$ [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism, def-weil-etale-morphism] of rank $p^a$ (that is, $\dim_k\mathcal O(E)=p^a$), and an isomorphism of $k$-group schemes $$H\simeq\mathbf G_a^d\times\prod_{j=1}^s\alpha_{p^{r_j}}\times E.$$ Here $\alpha_{p^r}(R)=\{x\in R:x^{p^r}=0\}$ with addition for every commutative $k$-algebra $R$; explicitly $\alpha_{p^r}=\operatorname{Spec}(k[t]/(t^{p^r}))$, with comultiplication $t\mapsto t\otimes1+1\otimes t$, counit $t\mapsto0$ and antipode $t\mapsto-t$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-polynomial-ring, def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. Empty products are trivial group schemes. No smoothness or connectedness hypothesis is imposed on $H$.

source.place: Proposition 14.52, printed p.297, together with Definition 14.45, printed p.295: elementary unipotent means admitting a closed embedding in a finite additive group power. Combine the finitely many additive factors and the finitely many etale factors; omit trivial factors alpha_(p^0).

proof.text: The given closed embedding $H\hookrightarrow\mathbf G_a^n$ puts $H$ in the class of groups to which primitive-function reconstruction applies, with no smoothness or connectedness assumption. Put $A=k_\sigma[F]$ and $M=P(H)$ as in that lemma. It supplies finite generation of the left $A$-module $M$ and the group-scheme isomorphism $H\simeq U(M)$.

source.place: Proposition 14.52, printed p.297; Theorem 14.46, Proposition 14.51 (corrected as reported), and Proposition 11.3. The steps expand the cyclic-factor calculation, including mixed inseparable/etale factors.

proof.text: Apply cyclic decomposition to $M$, using the stated perfection of $k$, to obtain $M\simeq\bigoplus_{i=1}^q A/Ag_i$. For every $k$-algebra $R$, restriction to the summands and summation are inverse maps between $\operatorname{Hom}_A(\bigoplus_i A/Ag_i,R)$ and $\prod_i\operatorname{Hom}_A(A/Ag_i,R)$. They commute with algebra maps and addition. With the representing group schemes supplied by reconstruction, these mutually inverse natural maps give $H\simeq\prod_i U(A/Ag_i)$. This also covers $q=0$, giving the trivial group.

source.place: Proposition 14.52, printed p.297; Theorem 14.46, Proposition 14.51 (corrected as reported), and Proposition 11.3. The steps expand the cyclic-factor calculation, including mixed inseparable/etale factors.

proof.text: An $A$-linear map $A/Ag\to R$ is determined by $x$, the image of $1$: it sends the class of $h$ to $h\cdot x$. It is well-defined exactly when $g\cdot x=0$, since $(ag)\cdot x=a\cdot(g\cdot x)$. Thus for $g=\sum_{j=0}^m c_jF^j$ the group $U(A/Ag)$ is the kernel of the additive polynomial $L_g(T)=\sum_j c_jT^{p^j}$ on $\mathbf G_a$, represented by $\operatorname{Spec}k[T]/(L_g)$. Indeed maps from this quotient to $R$ are exactly choices of $x$ with $L_g(x)=0$, naturally in $R$, and the group law is addition. For $g=0$ this is $\mathbf G_a$. A nonzero constant $g=c$ gives $L_g=cT$ and hence the trivial group.

source.place: Proposition 14.52, printed p.297; Theorem 14.46, Proposition 14.51 (corrected as reported), and Proposition 11.3. The steps expand the cyclic-factor calculation, including mixed inseparable/etale factors.

proof.text:
For a remaining nonzero $g$, let $m$ be its largest index with $c_m
e0$ and $r$ its smallest. Replace all $c_j$ by $c_m^{-1}c_j$; this scales $L_g$ by a unit, does not change its kernel, and makes it monic of degree $p^m$. The monic-quotient basis gives its kernel $K_g$ coordinate dimension $p^m$, so $K_g$ is finite. Factor $L_g=T^{p^r}u(T)$ with $u(0)=c_r
e0$. In $k[T]/(T^{p^r})$, $u$ has an inverse $v$: expand the finite geometric series for $u/c_r=1+T w$. Thus $uv+T^{p^r}w_1=1$ for a polynomial $w_1$. The map $k[T]/(L_g)	o k[T]/(T^{p^r})	imes k[T]/(u)$ has inverse $(a,b)\mapsto a\,uv+b\,T^{p^r}w_1$ modulo $L_g$. This explicit open-and-closed decomposition identifies the identity component with $\operatorname{Spec}k[T]/(T^{p^r})$: its first factor has just the prime $(T)$, and the other factor has no identity point because $u(0)
e0$. Its inclusion has the additive group law, so $K_g^\circ=\alpha_{p^r}$. For $r=0$, this means the trivial group $\alpha_1$.

source.place: Proposition 14.52, printed p.297; Theorem 14.46, Proposition 14.51 (corrected as reported), and Proposition 11.3. The steps expand the cyclic-factor calculation, including mixed inseparable/etale factors.

proof.text: The finite commutative group $K_g$ is over the original perfect field, so reduced splitting gives $K_g\simeq K_g^\circ\times E_g$ with $E_g=(K_g)_{\mathrm{red}}$ finite etale. Inserting the identity component just computed gives $K_g\simeq\alpha_{p^r}\times E_g$. The coordinate ring of this product is $\mathcal O(E_g)[T]/(T^{p^r})$; its monic power basis gives $\dim_k\mathcal O(K_g)=p^r\dim_k\mathcal O(E_g)$. Since the left side is $p^m$, the rank of $E_g$ is $p^{m-r}$. This includes $r=m$, when its rank is $1$, and $r=0$, when all of $K_g$ is etale.

source.place: Proposition 14.52, printed p.297; Theorem 14.46, Proposition 14.51 (corrected as reported), and Proposition 11.3. The steps expand the cyclic-factor calculation, including mixed inseparable/etale factors.

proof.text: Collect the factors $g_i=0$ into $\mathbf G_a^d$, discard the trivial constant factors and the factors $\alpha_1$, and list the positive remaining values of $r$ as $r_1,\ldots,r_s$. Let $E=\prod_i E_{g_i}$ over the nonzero factors, and put $a=\sum_i(m_i-r_i)$. The projection from a two-factor product to its second factor is a base change of the first factor's structure morphism, hence etale; composing with the second structure morphism is etale. Iteration proves etaleness of $E$. Affine fibre products have tensor-product coordinate rings. The tensor products of the finite bases span, and applying the dual coordinate functionals shows their linear independence. Thus $E$ is finite by the affine definition and so $\dim_k\mathcal O(E)=\prod_i p^{m_i-r_i}=p^a$. Associating and permuting the displayed product isomorphisms gives precisely the required isomorphism. If no such factors occur, take $E=\operatorname{Spec}k$ and $a=0$.

lean.statement: theorem additive_subgroup_perfect_decomposition {k : Type u} [Field k] (p : ℕ) [CharP k p] (hp : 0 < p) (hperfect : ∀ x : k, ∃ y : k, y ^ p = x) (n : ℕ) (H : Grp (Over (Spec (.of k)))) (i : H ⟶ ∏ᶜ fun _ : Fin n ↦ Grp.mk (StandardGroupSchemes.additive k)) [IsClosedSubgroupScheme i.hom.hom] [LocallyOfFiniteType H.X.hom] [QuasiCompact H.X.hom] : ∃ (d s a : ℕ) (r : Fin s → ℕ), (∀ j : Fin s, 1 ≤ r j) ∧ ∃ (A : Fin s → Grp (Over (Spec (.of k)))) (E : Grp (Over (Spec (.of k)))), (∀ j : Fin s, ∃ e : (A j).X ≅ StandardGroupSchemes.alpha k (p ^ r j), IsMonHom (e.hom ≫ StandardGroupSchemes.alphaInclusion k (p ^ r j))) ∧ IsCommMonObj E.X ∧ IsFinite E.X.hom ∧ Etale E.X.hom ∧ E.X.hom.finrankΓ = p ^ a ∧ Nonempty (H ≅ ((∏ᶜ fun _ : Fin d ↦ Grp.mk (StandardGroupSchemes.additive k)) ⨯ (∏ᶜ fun j : Fin s ↦ A j)) ⨯ E)
